title: Did God not know, and the close of the sixth book
source_text: Οὐκ οἶδα δ᾿ ὅπως φησὶ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ὅτι ὁ πάντα εἰδὼς τοῦτο οὐκ ἠπίστατο, ὅτι κακοῖς ἀνθρώποις καὶ ἁμαρτησομένοις καὶ κολάσουσιν αὐτοῦ τὸν υἱὸν πέμπει. ἀλλ᾿ ἔοικε νῦν μὲν ἑκὼν ἐπιλελῆσθαι τοῦ φάσκοντος λόγου πάντα, ἃ πείσεται Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς, προεωρακέναι θείῳ πνεύματι, καὶ πεπροφητευκέναι τοὺς τοῦ θεοῦ προφήτας· οἷς οὐχ ἕπεται τὸ μὴ ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεὸν ὅτι κακοῖς καὶ ἁμαρτησομένοις ἀνθρώποις πέμπει τὸν υἱὸν καὶ κολάσουσιν αὐτόν. εὐθέως δὲ λέγει τὸ πάλαι ταῦτα προειρῆσθαι ἐν ἀπολογίᾳ ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λέγεσθαι. ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν εἴληφεν ὁ ἕκτος ἡμῶν τόμος, αὐτοῦ που καταπαύσαντες τὸν λόγον ἀρξόμεθα θεοῦ διδόντος ἑβδόμου· ἐν ᾧ ἀπαντᾶν νομίζει πρὸς τὸ ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λέγεσθαι τοὺς προφήτας πάντα τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ προειρηκέναι. ἅπερ ἐπεὶ πλείονά ἐστι καὶ πλείονος λόγου δεῖται τοῦ πρὸς αὐτὰ, οὔτε διακόψαι ἐβουλήθημεν ὑπὸ τοῦ μεγέθους ἀναγκαζόμενοι τοῦ βιβλίου οὔτε ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ διακόψαι τὸν λόγον μέγιστον ποιῆσαι καὶ ὑπὲρ τὸ σύμμετρον τὸν ἕκτον τόμον.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know how he says (φησί) about God that 'the one knowing all (ὁ πάντα εἰδώς) did not understand (ἠπίστατο) this, that to wicked (κακοῖς) humans, both about to sin (ἁμαρτησομένοις) and about to punish (κολάσουσιν), he sends his Son.' But he seems now willingly (ἑκών) to have forgotten (ἐπιλελῆσθαι) the word/teaching (λόγος) which says that all things which Jesus the Christ would suffer (πείσεται) the prophets of God foresaw (προεωρακέναι) by divine spirit (θείῳ πνεύματι) and prophesied (πεπροφητευκέναι); from which it does not follow (οὐχ ἕπεται) that God had not known that he sends the Son to wicked and about-to-sin humans who would also punish him. Immediately (εὐθέως) he says that the 'these were foretold long ago (πάλαι προειρῆσθαι)' is said by us in defence (ἐν ἀπολογίᾳ). But since our sixth volume (τόμος) has taken a sufficient compass (αὐτάρκη περιγραφήν), stopping the discourse somewhere here we will begin, God granting (θεοῦ διδόντος), the seventh, in which he thinks to meet (ἀπαντᾶν) our saying that the prophets foretold all the things about Jesus. Which since they are many and need more discourse in reply, we neither wished to cut off (διακόψαι), compelled by the size of the book, nor, in order not to cut off the discourse, to make the sixth volume very large and beyond due measure (ὑπὲρ τὸ σύμμετρον).
pass_b_english: I do not know how he can say of God: “He who knows all things did not understand this, that he was sending his Son to wicked men, who would sin and would punish him.” But it seems that here he has deliberately forgotten our teaching, which says that the prophets of God foresaw by the divine Spirit everything that Jesus Christ would suffer, and foretold it. From this it does not follow that God did not know that he was sending his Son to wicked men, who would sin and would punish him. Yet in the very next breath he says that our claim that these things were foretold long ago is something we say in self-defence.

But since our sixth book has reached a sufficient length, we will end the argument about here, and, if God grants it, we will begin the seventh. In it Celsus thinks he is answering our statement that the prophets foretold everything about Jesus. These matters are many and need a longer reply, and so we did not wish either to break the discussion off, forced by the size of the book, or, so as not to break off the argument, to make the sixth book very long and out of proportion.

choices.choice: Celsus’s sentence ‘He who knows all things...’ is given as a direct quotation, as Origen introduces it with φησὶ... ὅτι; it may have been a question in Celsus (‘Did he who knows all things not understand...?’), but Origen’s reply treats it as a claim. The later remark (‘our claim... is something we say in self-defence’) is reported indirectly and is not put in quotation marks. νῦν μὲν... εὐθέως δέ marks Origen’s point that Celsus forgets the prophecies here, yet at once mentions our claim that they were foretold; rendered ‘here... Yet in the very next breath’. ἑκών rendered ‘deliberately’. ‘Our teaching’ renders τοῦ φάσκοντος λόγου (the account that says); ‘our’ is implied by the context. θείῳ πνεύματι capitalised as ‘the divine Spirit’ because it means the Spirit of prophecy, God’s Spirit. The idea that the prophets foretold Christ’s sufferings by the Spirit may recall 1 Peter 1:11, but no wording is quoted; possible allusion, not cited. διακόψαι (‘break off, interrupt’) rendered ‘break off’, not ‘cut short’, since Origen means splitting the discussion between books, not abridging it. τόμος rendered ‘book’.
νῦν μὲν... εὐθέως δέ contrast restored: 'for the moment' -> 'here', 'He goes on at once' -> 'Yet in the very next breath'
θεοῦ διδόντος: 'God granting' -> 'if God grants it'
διακόψαι: 'cut them short' / 'cut the argument short' -> 'break the discussion off' / 'break off the argument' (splitting, not abridging)

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
